summary: Both designs fit the brief well and converge on a safe, gentle five-stop market walk. Design Y is slightly stronger overall because it makes accessibility and the social ending more concrete, while Design X is more spatially precise in its prototype. Both contain a scoring/time inconsistency that should be removed.

differences.design_x: Prototype tests whether the loop causes dizziness, and specifies a 1.2 m corridor and 0.6 m edge clearance.
differences.design_y: Prototype additionally tests early discomfort, shortened steps, reaching for walls/staff, and whether chest-height signs can be read without bending; it also offers a seated computer alternative for unsteady walkers.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype: “test_questions” asks about dizziness; Design Y prototype: “test_questions” explicitly observes balance behaviours and readability, while “decisions” includes an alternative for players with unstable walking.

differences.design_x: Prototype sketch includes seven route coordinates, explicit audience zones on both sides, radii, and a path that returns to its start.
differences.design_y: Prototype sketch identifies a route and zones but gives fewer stop positions than its stated five stops: its first story zone combines the market-front greeting and grocery stop.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype “sketch” lists five distinct story zones plus start/goal and audience zones. Design Y prototype “mechanics” and final plan require five checkpoints, but its “sketch.zones” has only four story zones.

differences.design_x: Uses five familiar physical-market vignettes, ending with a canal bridge and an exit near the start; spectators can direct the player if wanted.
differences.design_y: Builds toward an old-radio pause and explicitly returns the player to friends, followed by sharing memories after headset removal.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype storyboard ends at “สะพานไม้ริมคลอง” (wooden bridge by the canal). Design Y prototype storyboard ends with “เสียงจากวันวาน” (sounds from the past) at the radio, then asks players to tell friends what it reminded them of; its final plan places the portal near south-side seating.

differences.design_x: Says there is no time pressure, but prototype decisions award a time bonus.
differences.design_y: Says there is no timer or in-play score, but prototype decisions say the system scores checkpoints and time, even if hidden.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype “decisions”: “300 points plus a time bonus.” Design Y prototype “decisions”: “scores according to checkpoints and time,” while its HUD says no score or timer. Both final build plans remove the scoring display/time limit.

differences.design_x: The timed flow assigns roughly 30–40 seconds to each stop and reaches completion at 4:00, despite allowing rest at every stop.
differences.design_y: Likewise schedules completion at 4:00, but its option explicitly flags that slow puzzle play could exceed four minutes; the selected walk still permits unrestricted pauses.
differences.evidence: Both prototype “flow” sections finish at 4:00 and promise optional rests. Design Y’s second option “risks” explicitly identifies the duration issue, but neither selected-plan build document explains what happens if a player pauses longer.

why: Design Y turns the brief’s social and first-time-user needs into clearer testing and a meaningful return-to-friends ending. Design X remains the better reference for exact route implementation. The margin is small because both selected designs are highly similar and both need the hidden time-based scoring removed.
x_weaknesses: The four-minute flow is too rigid if rest is genuinely unrestricted.
Its ending is less explicitly connected to post-play conversation with friends.
y_weaknesses: The prototype sketch does not visibly represent all five required checkpoints.
Hidden time-based scoring contradicts its stated no-timer/no-score experience.
The seated computer alternative is useful, but it changes platform/mode and needs an equivalently designed accessibility path.
improvements: Remove all score and time-bonus logic from both designs; reward completion with a calm closing message instead.
Define a flexible session end: staff can finish at any stop and escort the player to the exit without failure.
For Design Y, revise the sketch so all five stops have distinct, physically plausible locations and clearance.
For Design X, retain its measured layout but add Design Y’s balance/readability observations and structured post-play memory-sharing prompt.
